items: Search your state's Contractors State License Board website using the license number the contractor provides to verify their license is active, current, and matches the name on your contract.
Request a Certificate of Insurance directly from the contractor's insurer and verify that their general liability policy holds at least $1 million in coverage.
Contact your Secretary of State or county clerk to confirm the contractor's business is registered, how long they've operated, and who the registered agent is.
Before signing anything, confirm the license holder's name matches the business name on the contract exactly, since scammers frequently use names very similar to legitimate firms.
Never pay more than one-third of the total project cost upfront, regardless of how eager the contractor is to begin work immediately.
Insist on paying by check, credit card, or a protected payment platform and never pay in cash, since cash offers no fraud protection or documentation trail.
Hold the final one-third of payment until project completion and your written sign-off, with the middle third paid only after you physically verify meaningful progress at the project midpoint.
Require a lien waiver clause in your contract to protect yourself from subcontractors placing liens on your home if the contractor fails to pay their suppliers or workers.
Include a detailed scope of work in your contract that specifies all materials, brands, and quantities, so you have documented proof of exactly what was promised.
Add concrete start and completion dates to your contract instead of vague timelines like "as soon as possible," since dated milestones trigger your right to terminate.
Document the change order process in your contract requiring that any extra work or charges must be pre-approved and added to the contract in writing before additional work begins.
Refuse to sign any waiver that releases the contractor from liability, since these documents eliminate your legal recourse if the work is defective or incomplete.
